#1069. Mauricio Pochettino's final go with USMNT is all about pivoting to the future before Manchester United move

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Three days after tearing up as he announced his departure from the U.S. men's national team, outgoing head coach Mauricio Pochettino said he does not want to think about the emotions that will hit him once the job comes to an end with Tuesday's Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal against Haiti. He preached that it's still business as usual, even as one unusual week comes to a close and another equally unusual week begins.

After two years of answering questions about Pochettino's future as different European clubs took an interest in his services, his decision last week to join Manchester United finally offered them a semblance of clarity. The task in front of them on Tuesday is a simple one, especially after Saturday's 6-0 win over Haiti in the first leg – play like Pochettino's version of the U.S. team one last time.

"For me, tomorrow is about play[ing] like the tie is 0-0," he said on Monday in his penultimate press conference before returning to England. "I don't want to be disappointed. I don't want to lose the focus. I don't want to be less concentrated … [If] you take the game in a way that says it's not important tomorrow because it's already done, I think you will pay in the future – that lack of respect to the competition, to the opponent, to the result, to yourself. That is why tomorrow what I want is I'm going to put the best team possible and to perform."

Pochettino has been hesitant to reflect on his legacy after two years with the USMNT but that has been a common refrain during his tenure, spending just as much time molding the team's mentality in his image as he has their style of play. He leaves behind a mixed track record – results were all over the place in the build-up to the World Cup but it all appeared to come together once the tournament started, only for the U.S. team to fall flat on their faces in a round of 16 exit forever tinged by the Folarin Balogun affair. The stakes are undoubtedly lower against Haiti, the first leg advantage so substantial that the USMNT can probably survive another unimpressive performance before closing the book on the Pochettino years. There's a hint of succession planning in his plans for Tuesday, though, even if those plans are no longer his to execute.

"What I hope is to create the same link with us, with the new coaches that arrive here," Pochettino said. "It's to create the same link with the players. [It's] become an emotional relationship, that you can find the best for this group of players that have enormous talent … That is an official game and it's the opportunity to keep growing for the future, to settle all the principles and grow and grow and grow."

For all his faults and shortcomings, Pochettino does leave the national team in better shape than he found it. Some of it is out of his control – up and comers like Julian Hall, who scored on Saturday and now has four goals in his first five games for the senior team, were very likely poised for success no matter who the USMNT head coach was. After much trial and tribulation, though, he implemented a clear style of play and a cultural shift that several players have championed over the last week. Tuesday's game is ultimately a showcase for the players who will remain long after Pochettino leaves, both on an individual level as they aim to impress whoever takes the helm and as they try to prove a collective point now that the Pochettino years are over. U.S. Soccer's financial might may help sway Pochettino's eventual successor to take the job, no matter who that might be, but there is a pure soccer argument to taking this job.

For perhaps the first time in its modern history, the USMNT can prioritize style of play with their next hire. That's true outside the reported approach for ex-Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola, whose interest in the job is unclear. Pochettino's high-intensity, attack-minded version of the U.S. team suited the players at this year's World Cup and feels especially tailor-made for the rising talents headlined by Cavan Sullivan, the 17-year-old Philadelphia Union attacker who is now MLS' youngest-ever MVP nominee. A strong outing on Tuesday will allow the Pochettino years to look like a stepping stone to an important new chapter, one that will hopefully get the best out of the experienced players as well as their younger teammates, no matter who oversees the project.

As for Pochettino, laying the groundwork for the USMNT's future comes while he focuses on his own. Assistant coach Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez and sports scientist Sebastiano Pochettino departed for Manchester after Saturday's win over Haiti at Miami's Nu Stadium, filling in the gaps before Pochettino departs Cincinnati on Wednesday to begin his new role. The rest of his coaching staff will stay in Ohio to finish out the international break with the USMNT before traveling alongside Pochettino.

Two years removed from starting a new job with a short runway, Pochettino will do so again at United. The earliest he can oversee his first training session with United is Thursday, three days before an all-important clash with Liverpool. The longtime London resident, who previously coached Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea, insists he will not be out of the loop when he finally makes his Premier League return.

"For me, it's not difficult," he said of the quick turnaround. "I think we are well prepared to switch quick to like a player, from the national team to the clubs, from one game that you don't play well to another that you need to be ready again, from one action to the next action. I think we are well-prepared and then all the experience from the past, I think, helps us to be focused in the priority of the moment that demands that business. Today is to be focusing here in Cincinnati for the game against Haiti tomorrow but for sure, in the moment that game [finishes], we are going to start to be 100% focused in our next project … We watch soccer every day, all the leagues and we are always because that is our passion, our passion. We know the team [very well]. We know every single team [very well] and I think we don't need to match the preparation about the opponent. The most important [thing] is to know the details about our players, our staff, our culture, our identity and from there, to improve but now we are focusing [on] that game and we want to finish well tomorrow."

A large task awaits Pochettino at United, who are currently in the relegation zone with just one win from their opening 10 league games of the season.

#1067. Diego Kochen shows poise in USMNT net as young goalkeeper stakes claim to starting job

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Historically, goalkeeper has been a position of strength for the United States men's national team, to the extent that during the time of Tim Howard and Brad Guzan, both were playing Premier League soccer, but only one could start between the sticks. Things have changed since then, with numerous keepers coming through the ranks over the years, with most playing domestically or sitting on the bench for stronger European sides. However, that could be coming to an end for the team.

During Mauricio Pochettino's tenure, Matt Freese has been his starting keeper, taking over during the Gold Cup and starting every game that he was available for until the September/October international window, when Pochettino used Diego Kochen and Brian Schwake. Kochen, who is playing his first season of first-team soccer at Lyngby in Denmark (where center back Neil Pierre also got his first taste of senior soccer), got the clean sheet against Mexico during that camp and turned that into a start against Haiti in Concacaf Nations League play in his native Miami, setting the USMNT up well to advance to the semifinals of the tournament.

Following that match, Kochen acknowledged that the USMNT squad has done a lot to put him in this position, and he'll know that even if Pochettino won't be the manager choosing the lineups, performances like this one will be important for how the USMNT keeper picture looks moving forward.

"I feel like I've grown quite a lot," Kochen said following the match, reflecting on his adjustment to the national team. "I'm getting used to competing at the international level, but I've just got to give it to my team because they've been unbelievable. They make it so easy to just come out here and play free and be me, so without them, this wouldn't be possible."

His growth is evident; one of the first things that comes to mind when watching the 20-year-old is his poise. Kochen had the ball at his feet plenty, completing all 20 of his passes to help send the attack on its way, and also made the two saves that he needed to on a mostly quiet night. His age also showed when Haiti scored with him out of position, a goal that was called back for offside, but you take the good with the bad for young players because that's a learning moment, and as he earns more reps at the senior level, those are the kind of mistakes that can be ironed out.

"I'm not saying he hasn't played games in Barcelona, but at the senior level, every game he plays, he gets better and better and better," one of Kochen's coaches, Andreas Bjelland, told CBS Sports. "Because understanding the full-pitch play, and not only being on the line, just taking shots, and being a training goalie, but now he's playing for points every week. He's growing as a player, as a person, and as somebody we can trust more and more in the stuff we do. So it's nice to see that it has come to this ... It's quite impressive."

You can't teach poise, and spending more than five years in the Barcelona system shows in how Kochen carries himself. It's becoming more common in American soccer for young players to test themselves abroad or to get into Major League Soccer teams at a younger age, and when they succeed, it goes a long way developmentally, as Kochen's case shows.

"He is a person who trusts himself a lot. That's also why he's a good goalie, that at such a young age he hasn't that big of a doubt of himself," Mikkel Jespersen, Lyngby's other coach said. "He knows what he's capable of doing, and that's really important as a goalie: that you trust yourself and know what things you are doing is something that can succeed in a longer period."

While it's unknown what the next USMNT manager will value in a keeper, being able to perform in an uncertain environment with your coach having one foot out the door is something that will go a long way for Kochen's chances. In keeper terms, Kochen has plenty of time ahead of him, as players at his position regularly play until their late 30s or early 40s, so if he can continue this trajectory, the question of who protects the net could be solved for the foreseeable future.

Of course, that's a lot of projecting, but when the next generation of the USMNT is developing at an astounding rate, it's only natural to think about where players like Kochen could end up. Doing this in only his first season of professional soccer is already impressive, but the best is yet to come.

#1066. Arsenal's silent flaw of switching off could bite them hard against Europe's best - it's not sustainable and they were made to pay again in Borussia Dortmund draw, writes ISAAN KHAN

Published: 17:22 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 19:04 EST, 24 November 2026

Whether through complacency, boredom, or a mixture of both, Arsenal's habit of switching off in the second half of matches is becoming a serious issue.

It is a flaw which could bite them hard against teams they would encounter in the later stages of the Champions League.

When Kepa Arrizabalaga parried Julian Ryerson's shot into the path of Jobe Bellingham, the Arsenal script had seemingly flipped from first-half domination to second-half capitulation.

Luckily for Mikel Arteta, Bellingham's tap-in was flagged for offside to keep the north London club's unbeaten record in this competition intact, stretching back to 20 matches (excluding penalty shootouts).

Earlier in the second half, Maximilian Beier had equalised, skilfully turning Gabriel before placing a neat strike past Kepa.

But this match should have been sealed well before then for Arsenal - and they had enough chances to win it late on, too. Viktor Gyokeres headed wide when unmarked and Declan Rice struck the woodwork.

Arsenal were made to pay for their complacency again by drawing with Borussia Dortmund

Arsenal were held 1-1 with Dortmund thanks to this Maximilian Beier's strike for the visitors

By full-time, the Gunners had mustered 30 shots, but no winning goal.

Despite his team's wastefulness, Arteta said: 'The domination and threat was really impressive. The general feeling inside the dressing room is that we should reward ourselves with more. I love the courage, the fluidity and the understanding with the players with and without the ball.'

But the recurrence of losing concentration later in matches, as the Gunners did against Slavia Prague and Newcastle in recent weeks, is an issue which Arteta must urgently address.

It is not sustainable, and ruined an evening initially lit up by Gyokeres' stunning strike. The Sweden striker's display reflected the fierce competition for places at Arsenal. Perform well and you have a chance of a starting spot. Anything less results in a place on the bench in the winter's cold.

Gyokeres received Noni Madueke's pass outside the area on ten minutes and Dortmund's back line completely backed off, almost pleading for him to shoot.

He obliged, cocking his right boot back to unleash a powerful strike which initially looked to be going over the bar before dipping into goalkeeper Gregor Kobel's net. It was a top-drawer finish from a man who cannot nail down a regular starting spot, despite 21 goals last season and a goal and assist in Arsenal's previous Champions League match against Slavia Prague.

It is the kind of luxury Arteta has worked towards since taking on this job seven years ago.

One back-up player who inspires rather less confidence is goalkeeper Kepa. No1 David Raya injured his shoulder at Newcastle and so in came his fellow Spaniard. Kepa's touches early on were cheered by the Arsenal faithful, massaging the confidence of a man who has endured the kind of calamity which is not easily erased from memory.

The dropping of Rayan Cherki's cross in March's Carabao Cup final defeat by Manchester City; his lapse to misjudge a corner and gift Real Betis a goal during pre-season - these are the sorts of errors which have Arsenal fans feeling uncomfortable whenever Raya is unavailable.

Viktor Gyokeres (left) opened the scoring with this stunning long-range strike for the Gunners

Kepa Arrizabalaga (right) started in goal for Arsenal with first-choice David Raya out injured

Arsenal (4-2-3-1): Arrizabalaga 6; White 6 (Timber 65, 6), Konsa 6, Gabriel 5, Hincapie 6; Lewis-Skelly 5 (Guimaraes 66, 6), Rice 7; Madueke 8, Odegaard 7, Tzolis 5 (Eze 66, 6); Gyokeres 7.

Borussia Dortmund (3-4-2-1): Kobel 6; Gadou 7, Anton 6, Schlotterbeck 6; Ryerson 6, Nmecha 6, Veerman 6, Svensson 6; Bellingham 6, Beier 7 (Guirassy 65, 6); Fabio Silva 6 (Karetsas 65, 6).

Raya is battling to return for Arsenal's huge Premier League clash against Manchester City on Sunday and the sense of panic in the days after his injury has been understandable.

Raya is so much more than just an excellent shot-stopper. His distribution is second to none: pinpoint long throws to set wingers away on counter-attacks and a highly impressive passing range, both aerially and across the floor.

Still, Kepa just about survived. There were jitters, like passing the ball straight to a yellow shirt on 52 minutes, which the opposition failed to punish. But he hung in there and that will have given his confidence a boost.

Arsenal started well, Madueke continuing his excellent form of late in place of the injured Bukayo Saka. Madueke crossed for Christos Tzolis, who drove his shot into the turf, before setting up Martin Odegaard to shoot wide.

It didn't take long for the winger's passing to produce results, as he fed Gyokeres for that venomous strike from distance.

Rice lashed a strike from range which dipped just over the bar as Dortmund showed a tendency to gift too much time on the ball.

After the break Dortmund changed tack. Sitting back and soaking up the pressure was not working, so they got the ball forward more quickly and more often, forcing Arsenal on to the back foot.

The Gunners held on for a point - and endured another lesson in switching off.

There is no more room for error in the 2026-27 UEFA Women's Champions League. After four matchdays, the league phase has been whittled down to only two games left for each of the 18 clubs, and the margin between a bye into the quarterfinals and an extra round of knockout playoffs in February will come down to dwindling points.

OL Lyonnes rule the league phase at the moment. They top the tournament table with ten points, level with FC Barcelona but with a superior goal difference. Just behind the two Champions League contenders are Bayern Munich and Arsenal, with Chelsea FC and Manchester City creeping closer to the top four. Out of the 18 clubs competing, only four will earn direct berths to the quarterfinals, and eight will compete for a future spot alongside them.

The final six clubs with the least amount of points will see their Champions League dream end, so matchday 5 will be a crucial turning point for several teams.

Fighting for top spot positioning will be Arsenal and OL Lyonnes, and Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain. HB Koge, Roma, and tournament debutants Inter Milan are level on four points and need to be in full urgency mode if they're to leapfrog and remain in contention for future rounds.

CHRISTIAN PULISIC GET ON YOUR BIKE‼️#USMNT x @VW pic.twitter.com/Yb3yqXfC33

Julian Hall followed with a poacher's goal as Weston McKennie played orchestrator, and it continued a theme that whoever ends up taking over the national team will have tough decisions ahead. Folarin Balogun is struggling for minutes with Monaco and is looking to make a move at the end of the season, and Hall has done everything that he can to increase his own standing with five goals in six games for the USMNT.

The New York Red Bulls star has a ways to go considering that he's still only 18 and will need to gain experience against top teams in the world instead of just Haiti, but he also can't ask for a better start than what he has gotten off to. It's why this is such an attractive job for whoever takes over the USMNT. They'll be able to build upon the good that Pochettino has instilled; the talent is there to move the squad forward, and there's plenty to love about the youth of the USMNT.

And alongside that, Pulisic has essentially screamed don't forget about me. During this camp, the Milan man has followed up on signing a new contract with the club by reaching 35 national team goals, moving into fourth all time for the USMNT over Eric Wynalda. Diego Kochen added to the good vibes with a third straight clean sheet, and Neil Pierre was even able to be cap-tied against the nation that he's also eligible for as the full-circle moments were left and right.

Pulisic, the former 17-year-old phenom, was subbed off for Cavan Sullivan, the current 17-year-old phenom, and while the goal difference may have been larger in the first leg between these sides, this felt like a more measured performance despite the strangeness of Pochettino's assistants heading to United while he managed the squad prior to catching his own charter.

This camp had every chance of being a disaster given the circumstances of Pochettino leaving, but all parties did what was needed during this camp. All dual nationals were capped, including Santiago Castaneda, showing that even on his way out, Pochettino made sure to take care of the future of the federation. On to the next round of the Concacaf Nations League with a new manager and no complaints with the performance so far for the squad.

#1058. USWNT roster for Concacaf W Championship: Ashley Sanchez back, Sam Coffey returns, and Naomi Girma misses out

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest roster of the year for the U.S. women's national team is here. Head coach Emma Hayes has named a 23-player roster for the upcoming 2026 Concacaf W Championship.

The tournament serves as the World Cup qualifiers, and four teams will earn spots in the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup, with future Olympic spots also in play. Fans can watch all the Concacaf W Championship matches on Paramount+.

In just nine short days, eight teams will compete in a quarterfinal round. The U.S. and Canada earned direct byes into the tournament as Concacaf's top two ranked teams, and six teams now join them after a preliminary qualifying round. The USWNT will face El Salvador on Nov. 27 in the quarterfinal round, and if they advance, they'll clinch a spot in next year's World Cup. The other matchups are Canada against Panama, Mexico vs. Haiti, and Jamaica will play Costa Rica.

"It's been a great year of growth and learning for our team, and for a long time the focus has been on qualifying for the World Cup, so now that time has arrived," said Hayes.

"I want to see relentless consistency from our players, individually and as a team, and I want us to be elite in both penalty boxes. If we can achieve that, I'm confident those performances will carry us through to meet our standards and goals. This is my first Concacaf event and the first for many of our players, so we're all looking forward to the experience."

Hayes selected a full roster that features several players competing in their first-ever senior-level World Cup qualifying tournament, and a handful of veterans. Just eight of the 23 players selected were members of the 2022 Concacaf W Championship roster: forwards Mallory Swanson, Trinity Rodman, Sophia Wilson, and Ashley Sanchez; defender Emily Fox; and midfielders Lindsey Heaps, Rose Lavelle, and Sam Coffey -- who joined mid-tournament that year.

Coffey returns to the roster after missing two previous international windows while managing a lower-leg injury. Defender Naomi Girma is out as she continues to manage a lingering calf injury. The centerback has not featured with the national team since April, and has yet to play with Chelsea FC this season. Midfielder Olivia Moultrie is currently rehabbing from an ACL injury sustained in August. Other notable omissions on the roster are Jaedyn Shaw and Ally Sentnor, both of whom have been part of U23 and senior camps throughout the year.

This is just the third camp for the attacking line of "triple espresso" since the 2024 Olympics. If the trio starts a match during the Concacaf W Championship, it will be the first time they start a game together since the gold medal match. Both Swanson and Wilson have worked their way back into senior camps over the year following maternity leave.

Goalkeepers (3): Claudia Dickey (Seattle Reign FC; 12/0), Mandy McGlynn (Utah Royals FC; 6/0), Phallon Tullis-Joyce (Manchester United, ENG; 8/0)

Defenders (8): Tierna Davidson (Gotham FC; 72/3), Kate Del Fava (Utah Royals FC; 1/0), Emily Fox (Arsenal FC, ENG; 80/1), Avery Patterson (Houston Dash; 15/1), Tara Rudd (Washington Spirit; 12/0), Evelyn Shores (Angel City FC; 0/0), Gisele Thompson (Angel City FC; 12/0), Kennedy Wesley (San Diego Wave FC; 9/1)

Midfielders (6): Croix Bethune (Kansas City Current; 7/1), Sam Coffey (Manchester City, ENG; 46/5), Lindsey Heaps (Denver Summit FC; 180/40), Claire Hutton (Bay FC; 22/1), Rose Lavelle (Gotham FC; 124/29), Lily Yohannes (OL Lyonnes, FRA; 22/1)

Forwards (6): Michelle Cooper (Kansas City Current; 16/1), Trinity Rodman (Washington Spirit; 59/13), Ashley Sanchez (North Carolina Courage; 30/4), Mallory Swanson (Chicago Stars; 105/39), Alyssa Thompson (Chelsea FC, ENG; 34/4), Sophia Wilson (Portland Thorns FC; 65/25)

Ashley Sanchez's return to the roster comes after standout performances against Spain last window and a stellar 2026 NWSL regular season where she won the Golden Boot with 20 goals scored. She was also nominated for the 2026 NWSL MVP award. A positional shift to left winger and an outrageous amount of scoring have all led her back to the USWNT due to consistent performances, a key factor for Hayes with her large player pool.

"Be consistent first of all in performance. Ashley Sanchez wasn't on our radar, not because she isn't talented, but there were certain things we demanded from the performance that I think she has delivered in her game on a regular basis. So, I think that's the first thing. I think you've seen that includes Croix Bethune coming into this camp -- been outstanding in the number 10 position all year, and would have been in last camp as well if she was fit. You do have to consistently find consistent performances, particularly if you're a player that doesn't have credit in the bank," Hayes said.

As the World Cup gets nearer, finalizing a roster for the 2027 summer tournament is even closer. Things like consistent form and senior-level experience will come into play when naming a final 23 for the World Cup for Hayes.

"If you're a Mallory Swanson and delivered on a world stage on a regular basis for the national team, it does alter things slightly. No, we don't want players that are in our group that are in a place where they're not fighting to improve every day or be as competitive as they could possibly be, but I think when players have stacked and accumulated a lot of experience over a period of time, that is always going to put them in a steady position," Hayes explained.

"But it doesn't guarantee anything. I will be unafraid to leave anybody off that plane if I don't feel that they are applying themselves to put ourselves in the best possible position to compete. Which is why this upcoming camp, our job is to qualify for the World Cup, and so everything we have worked towards is ensuring that every player that comes in at camp makes sure they lift their level and they position the team to have the most positive outcome, regardless of the opponent. And I'd be demanding as much as I always do, but I have a big expectation from our senior players to step up."

El Salvador is the eighth-ranked team in the Concacaf W Championship and earned its spot following a preliminary qualifying round. The group is coached by manager Eric Acuña, who recently made headlines for harshly criticizing his players in a press conference following losses to Paraguay last month.

Still, Hayes and the staff aren't taking any opponent lightly no matter the rankings or state of the locker room.

"It's a team that knows is competing for something, so it doesn't matter the opponent; they're competing to go to a World Cup, and do I think that will be it will be demanding and taxing? And yes, I do. In many different ways, because the expectations are all on us. I think for them, it's how are they going to disrupt us and make it difficult? But they have two players in the front line that can cause a lot of problems, particularly in transition. So we have to set up for that," Hayes said.

"I think when it when it comes to the players, I've always championed creating positive environments for players. And yeah, I'm sad for the players to hear what they've gone through, but as always, I can't control that. I want the best for players all of the time in their environments, but I am here to represent the U.S. and try and help us qualify for the World Cup. So my focus is on that. Even if my heart goes out to the players and I think we still have a lot of work to do in the women's game to keep driving female-centered, female-lens environments where women can thrive."

#1056. Why U.S. Soccer's move to name Emma Hayes to the USMNT hiring committee makes sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – By the time U.S. Soccer confirmed Mauricio Pochettino's departure for Manchester United early Friday morning, the announcement itself was far from a surprise. The press release included the usual formalities – Steve Cherundolo, the U-23 U.S. men's national team head coach, would fill in for the Dec. 13 friendly against Jamaica that falls outside the FIFA international match calendar, and the assurance that the search for Pochettino's USMNT successor would begin shortly. Federation CEO J.T. Batson and COO Dan Helfrich will unsurprisingly lead the search, as will "the soccer leadership team at U.S. Soccer that includes" assistant sporting director Oguchi Onyewu. There was one unique detail tucked into the announcement, though.

Emma Hayes, the U.S. women's national team head coach, will also have a say in the matter.

Men's and women's national teams rarely overlap at any given federation, largely because there's little need for a crossover event. They operate on different calendars and in the best case scenarios, each team has dedicated members of staff. Hayes' name-drop as news of Pochettino's exit became official, then, is a unicorn-like sighting, even if U.S. Soccer often champions a spirit of collaboration between all of its national teams. It is uncommon for the head coach of one senior national team to help recruit a counterpart but in U.S. Soccer's case, it makes complete sense.

Hayes' coaching career, which spans two decades and two continents, means her inclusion on the federation's soccer leadership team is an obvious one. She is amongst the most respected soccer minds in the game, which easily makes her one of the most important people on U.S. Soccer's payroll no matter how you look at it. That will be especially true in a hiring process that has to conclude with a compelling follow-up act to Pochettino's splashy arrival two years ago. Her perspective might actually be vital in the process, which only adds to the intrigue of what's next for the USMNT.

"We have an extraordinary gift, which is a women's national team manager who's incredibly insightful, bright mind about the sport, who has a set of personal experiences and relationships that span the club and international game, the men's and women's game, the domestic and international club game, and who also has lived in the shoes of what it's like to be a U.S. national team senior coach," Helfrich told CBS Sports on Thursday. "It is a no-brainer that that mind and that voice has a really prominent seat at the table when we're talking about important moves for the federation."

USMNT coaches are rarely style hires; look no further than the list of people to hold the job on a full-time basis this century and the picture paints itself. The only thing Bruce Arena, Bob Bradley, Jurgen Klinsmann, Gregg Berhalter and Pochettino seem to have in common, outside of the job they all once held, is that they were all tasked with some sort of cultural reset depending on the task at hand. That likely will not be the case for Pochettino's successor, though, who will inherit a team with a clear style of play, a healthy mix of veteran players and rising talents and plenty of time on the clock until the next World Cup. The job will be defined in part by continuity, even with the necessary allowance for the new hire to put their unique spin on things.

That's where Hayes' expertise should play a crucial role, and the same goes for Onyewu. Hayes' tactical know-how makes her as qualified as anyone employed by U.S. Soccer to establish the right stylistic profile for the next USMNT coach, especially with the spirit of continuity in mind. Pochettino's track record with the U.S. team was mixed but at its best, his high-intensity, attack-minded approach suited the player pool really well and continues to do so. Hayes, a tactical pragmatist who prioritized attack-minded teams herself with Chelsea and the USWNT, will be more than able to help match candidates to the player pool they will spend the next several years working with. Hayes admitted as much on Wednesday when addressing the topic for the first time.

"I work really closely with J.T. in particular and even more so with Dan as we're growing to develop the American soccer movement and J.T. asked if I would be involved as a technical voice, to be involved with the process and I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men's national team coach," she said. "My role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job, albeit with the women's team, and that I've coached for a number of years and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why and like I said, I feel confident in the group that are being put together. I think it'll be a very thorough process. I think that's the most important part of it and like I said, I feel very embedded in what we're doing with the federation so it doesn't feel unusual to me so, like I've said many times, let's build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that's the important part and let's get it right."

That's especially true considering the fact that there are very few slam-dunk candidates to replace Pochettino. Pep Guardiola, months into a sabbatical after a decade with Manchester City, is an obvious target for U.S. Soccer but it is entirely unclear how interested he would be in the vacancy. If he's out of the running, the list of contenders with genuine international appeal dwindles quickly but it does not necessarily mean the list of worthy candidates vanishes with Guardiola. The hiring committee will need to be strategic in that case, both in terms of creating a list of contenders and then narrowing them down over the interview process, Hayes providing an important perspective along the way.

The jobs of the USMNT and the USWNT head coaches are hardly apples-to-apples but even then, one will still have an acute idea of what the other's job entails. There is inherent value in having a coach help in the process of hiring another coach, since they hold such singular positions – they are often treated as the be-all, end-all when it comes to their team's success, fairly or otherwise. She can also speak to the cadence of national teams, which varies greatly from the club game where coaches essentially work with their players every day during a long season.

"Everyone is aware of the major differences between coaching at the club level and international level, and the main difference is just time on the field and time with your players," Hayes told CBS Sports earlier this year when asked about Pochettino. "Every international coach would love to have more time with their team, but that's not the nature of the international calendar and it's something I know we both had to get used to and are still getting used to … I said a few times that it's almost like we are grandparents. We get to see the players for a week or so and then we send them back to their parents, which is their clubs."

Outside of her tactical expertise, though, Hayes represents U.S. Soccer's ambitious turn in recent years as much as Pochettino does. She was hired because of her reputation as a serial winner at Chelsea, where she won eight league titles and seven cups. She continued the trend in short order with the USWNT – two months after officially starting in the role, she won Olympic gold at the Paris Games in 2024. U.S. Soccer has equally ambitious goals for the men's team, though the timeline will understandably be longer for that program. They continue to target the USMNT's first World Cup quarterfinal appearance since 2002 but in between, they also hope to medal in the Olympics' men's soccer event, which is contested by U-23 teams, for the first time when the Games come to Los Angeles in 2028. More than many at the federation, Hayes has experience with the intangibles it takes to reach those heights and that's exactly why she was hired in the first place. It also reflects what U.S. Soccer's executives are looking for in the next USMNT head coach.

"The most important characteristic is someone with ambition that matches ours, which is high and so when you have, then, that high shared ambition, then you look for the experience, the talent, the understanding that accompanies that ambition," Helfrich said.

Beyond that, though, Hayes in particular has an idea of what the USMNT job might entail. She is the best of both worlds – she began her coaching career in the U.S. two decades ago and has a deep understanding of the American soccer landscape, but made a name for herself in her native England and can also bring a useful outsider's perspective. There is no perfect equivalent to Hayes waiting for the USMNT job since no coach with experience in the American game has truly broken into the top tiers of the sport just yet, the federation likely to settle for one or the other. Hayes' understanding of both orbits, though, makes her an important guiding force along the way. She might be the only qualified person to answer how much to weigh the insider's perspective with the accomplished outsider's point of view when looking for the next USMNT head coach, in large part because she is the only person who boasts an equal share of it.

Hayes' expertise alone means she will be as valuable a sounding board as any, to the point that it's hard to minimize her ability to offer input down to one or two straightforward things. There is one more thing Hayes might have that no one at U.S. Soccer does – easy access to some of the most notable coaches in the game.

Over the course of her successful 12-year tenure at Chelsea, Hayes became one of the most respected coaches in England. She became the first woman to win the Football Writers Association's Tribute Award in 2024 shortly before leaving England for the U.S., and has earned the praise of many of her counterparts in the men's game along the way. Out of anyone at U.S. Soccer, Hayes might actually have the most compelling list of phone numbers in her contacts. She has said Sir Alex Ferguson, a coaching legend if there ever was one after his storied 27-year tenure at Manchester United, calls her "from time to time." Hayes has been in touch with a handful of her contemporaries over the years, including those who have been on U.S. Soccer's radar at one point or another. In her 2024 book, "A Completely Different Game," Hayes said she heard from Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp after having an emergency hysterectomy because of endometriosis in 2022. The pair "sent me long messages, expressing deeply felt emotions," as did Graham Potter and David Moyes.

The rolodex is a covetable one, if ex-U.S. Soccer sporting director Matt Crocker can serve as an example. His greatest accomplishments during his three-year spell, which came to an end in April when he took a similar role with the Saudi Arabian Football Federation, were hiring Hayes and Pochettino. He had previously worked with Pochettino at Southampton a decade earlier, which made U.S. Soccer's approach easier when discussions started. Hayes' value exceeds her ability to hand her bosses a phone number but it is unlikely to go unnoticed at U.S. Soccer, who clearly understands the expertise she would bring to the search in a variety of ways.

#1054. How to make climate anxiety your superpower

Download the Nature Podcast 23 November 2026

Late last week the UN’s climate conference, COP31, failed to reach a consensus on its headline message. That news came on the heels of the UN acknowledging that the 1.5 ˚C warming limit set out in Paris will be breached. So, it’s easy to feel anxious in a world where it seems that not enough is being done about climate change. But is it possible to overcome such anxiety or even use it?

In the final episode of Cooked? I open up about my own climate anxiety and discover that there are still things that I can do to battle climate change. And how those small individual actions could potentially lead to more systemic change.

00:00 Can I do anything about my climate anxiety?

04:43 What the science says about ‘ecoanxiety’

11:35 Can individuals really do anything?

Net zero emissions won’t reverse climate change — some nations look to ‘net negative’

The rise of eco-anxiety: scientists wake up to the mental-health toll of climate change

This episode was written and produced by Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was the editor. Music was by Akio Jefferson, Jonathan Maiocco, Aerial Circles, and Lionel Cohen, and was provided by Triple Scoop Music via Getty Images. Thanks to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu and Elizabeth Howe for featuring in this episode.

Nick Petrić Howe: Hi mum, can you hear me okay?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you’ve been listening to this series, you’ll know that I’ve been struggling a bit with anxiety about the climate. If you’re just joining us now, hi, I’m Nick Petrić Howe and I have a climate anxiety problem. Throughout this series, I’ve spoken to a lot of scientists about the big ideas and big data that we can use to tackle climate change, but I haven’t really addressed the core reason of why I wanted to do this — to figure out what to do with my own feelings about climate change.

I wanted to know if I’d always felt this way, and if so, what I could do about it. So, I called up an expert on me. My mum.

Nick Petrić Howe: Can I record this call for work?

Elizabeth Howe: Yeah, course you can yeah

Nick Petrić Howe: Yeah? I just wanted to ask you something. When I was a kid, was I an anxious worried child would you say?

Nick Petrić Howe: This wasn’t exactly what I was expecting. I feel like I worry about things and have worried about them a lot throughout my life. But maybe there was something special about climate change, I know that it’s held a special position in my life. It’s why I decided to study biology when I finished school, eventually doing a PhD — to figure out if there was some way to help save the planet. So, I tried a different tack.

Nick Petrić Howe: Do you ever remember me worrying about, like, the environment and stuff. Elizabeth Howe: Oh God yeah. You were always thinking about stuff like that.

Elizabeth Howe: Well because you said— there was a big thing about climate change and you said ‘oh well climate change isn’t real because, you see, what happens is, in science, is that the world has these ice ages and then everything melts and then daa daa daa daaa.’ So you said, ‘it’s just a normal event, it’s not anything to do with global warming and it’s a load of rubbish.’ But you were always looking into stuff like that and listening to stuff like that. You were very interested in the scientific explanations for things.

Nick Petrić Howe: I’m not sure how I feel about that to be honest.

Nick Petrić Howe: Not gonna lie, being outed as a junior climate denier was not on my bingo card for this year. We eventually came to the conclusion that this was a phase I went through when I was quite young and hadn’t quite understood that people could just well… lie on national television. Misinformation, unfortunately, isn’t just a new thing. When I was a kid in the 90s, there were campaigns to make climate research seem a lot more questionable than now, and established politicians like Lord Nigel Lawson in the UK openly criticised the science.

At least, it seemed, I was interested in the climate. For the record, now I absolutely am convinced, along with the scientific community, that climate change is real and human caused.

And, even according to my mum, as I got older, I cared more about the climate, even if I wasn’t necessarily worried.

Elizabeth Howe: I don’t think you were particularly too worried…

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, I remember thinking when I was a teenager and I was more appraised of the actual facts, that climate change was a solvable problem. One that my generation could fix. I was filled with notions of all the things that science had accomplished — the moon landings, the internet, and general relativity — breakthroughs that solved problems once thought insurmountable. It took me getting older to become a bit more jaded, concerned that we’d not done enough soon enough and that maybe it was too late.

But this got me thinking, if I wasn’t worried once and even felt hopeful. Is that something I could recapture? This series has already taught me that in many ways we’ve done more than I thought to tackle climate change and that people are actively working on solutions. But that only goes so far to assuage my own anxiety. So you’ll forgive me if I spend this episode figuring out if there’s something that can help me. Is there anything I can do?

Nick Petrić Howe: As I said, I’ve struggled with anxiety about climate change. Sometimes I feel paralysed by how hopeless it all seems. There’s so much to do and it’s not getting done fast enough. At the same time, every other week there seems to be another climate record smashed or a natural disaster exacerbated by climate change.

It’s easy to feel anxious. So, in this third and final episode of Cooked? I wanted to know - am I normal? Or am I bit of an outlier here? Are other people having these feelings of hopelessness in the face of climate change.

So, I called up one of the world experts on how climate change is affecting mental health.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Emma Lawrance, from Imperial College London. After figuring out our settings, we connected on a slightly better line. And Emma told me that I’m by no means alone, in fact, it turns out there is a name for what I’m feeling. There’s a few actually.

Emma Lawrance: So there is this kind of emerging plethora of terms really that all centre on this kind of umbrella of what we might call psychological responses or emotional responses to the climate crisis. And so some of those terms can be things like climate related distress, climate anxiety, eco anxiety, ecological grief, solastalgia.

Nick Petrić Howe: And while there are differences between these terms, for the purposes of the podcast I’m just going to say eco-anxiety — the anxiety about climate change and environmental destruction, as that seems the most fitting with my experience.

And one of the first things that Emma impressed upon me is that there’s a lot we don’t know about eco-anxiety. This is a rapidly emerging field, but eco-anxiety is a thing that a lot of people are feeling. Especially if they’re dealing with the consequences of climate change.

Emma Lawrance: So for instance, in our sample of nearly 3,000 young people surveyed across the US, one fifth of the young people who didn't report experiencing a climate change-related event were afraid to have children that rose to one third of the young people who said they had already experienced a climate change-related event. And there was a correlation between the people sort of self-reporting and looking at their postcodes and where you know, climate hazards had been in the US. So, they seem to be kind of reflecting sort of a real-world experience.

Nick Petrić Howe: And that makes sense. If climate change is affecting you, then you would worry about it. I know my own anxiety spiked during the heatwaves, wildfires and droughts of this last British summer. But that does also mean that there are certain people who worry a bit more than others.

Emma Lawrance: There's more and more studies showing that eco-anxiety is definitely not like a white Western phenomenon. This experience of distress and what can be called eco-anxiety in response to changing climate is actually much higher in the countries and in the communities where these impacts are already occurring.

Nick Petrić Howe: That might surprise you, it certainly did me - In some ways, I had thought that maybe this was a worry more for people like me. Western, relatively well-off folks, who have time to worry about things. But, if my anxiety spiked over one record breaking summer, perhaps it shouldn’t be shocking that people facing these impacts week after week in the developing countries most effected, but least responsible for climate change are worried too. And they’re only getting more worried.

Emma Lawrance: It's happening in ways that are then compounding. So people are experiencing not just one, but multiple kind of stresses and disasters, often coming back-to-back and they're not having time to recover before the next one hits that experience into place with this awareness of, well, what's to come? The awareness of the injustice of the situation of often kind of insufficient climate action and power dynamics between, you know, the people who are affected and the people causing the problem and growing inequalities in some spaces or many spaces globally. those things are we're seeing this really rapid increase in the use of the term eco anxiety. So I think there's over a 4,000-fold percent increase in Google searches. five-year period. And so, it’s really skyrocketed

Nick Petrić Howe: Strangely, it feels a little better to know that I’m not alone in these feelings. Perhaps I am a bit more normal than I thought. But I wanted to know what could be done about these feelings. For me, the anxiety has sometimes been paralysing. I haven’t wanted to engage with climate news, which, as I’ve said, is a bit of a funny position to be in as a science journalist. And Emma explained to me that, for some people it can be like that. It can even affect people’s daily lives, and those people may need some extra help and support, but for many people this anxiety can be quite an understandable reaction.

Emma Lawrance: Eco-anxiety isn't something that the vast majority of researchers and people living with these experiences and profession and, mental health professionals would say needs to be a quote unquote, like diagnosis. And it's something that is, can be very rational. It's understandable, and often proportionate to feel alarm, to feel distressed, to feel the strong emotions in response to the facts of the climate crisis.

Nick Petrić Howe: And for some people, it may even be a feeling they want to hold onto. They can use it to push them to battle climate change.

Emma Lawrance: We also know that people who are feeling that distress are more likely to be taking pro-environmental action. We know that collective action, particularly rather than individual action can help you like hold high distress and protect your mental health and wellbeing. it's not sometimes holding distress can impact, you know, is related to poorer mental health, it's related to higher insomnia, et cetera. But young people are saying, you know, we don't want our distress to be taken away in a sense, because this shows that we care. It shows that we care about the world. It can be fuel for action, but that action needs to be often done with others. And also can for some people lead into action that ends up providing more meaning and joy and purpose and it can be a really good thing, but for others it can be overwhelming and paralysing and have really severe impacts on their life

Nick Petrić Howe: So, to my question of what I’m supposed to do with these feelings... I think I’m already doing it. These feelings can overwhelm, and I’ve certainly felt that. But maybe doing something is a way to help live with these anxious feelings. The question is though, what do you do?

Kimberly Nicholas: I really think if your listeners were taking these high-impact climate actions just 20 minutes a day. It would be enough.

Nick Petrić Howe: Now, what I don't want to do is make you feel as though the weight of the world is on your shoulders. Saying that you are ultimately responsible for climate change is too much of a burden for any one person to bear. As someone who worries a lot, I think that weight would crush me, frankly. It’s also fair to say that many of these problems are systemic too. Governments, nations, and businesses should all meet ambitious climate targets if we’re to avoid the worst consequences of climate change. And if you live in the US, say, even if you have very minimal emissions compared to your neighbours, you’re likely to have higher emissions than someone in Bangladesh — just because of how baked in carbon emissions are. If you have an electric car in the US, for example, it’s getting electricity from more fossil fuel power plants than someone in Norway. So, it’s easy to think that any individual action is a waste of time.

Kimberly Nicholas: Well, ineffective individual actions are a waste of time.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Kimberly Nicholas, a climate scientist at Lund University. And she’s someone who’s spent quite a bit of time thinking about what individuals can do, and perhaps what they shouldn’t do.

Kimberly Nicholas: We don't need to focus on recycling or canvas bags. People really have the wrong ideas about what individual action means. And so that I think is a myth that we need to dispel. So, it's not about doing everything, it's not that every little thing matters, it's that focusing our limited time and energy where it can really make a difference can lead us to take powerful actions today that do lead to system change.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just the what that Kimberly has been thinking about, it’s the who too.

Kimberly Nicholas: I really focus on this group that is in the top 10% globally, many of whom are surprised to learn that they are in that group. So if you earn over about 38,000 US dollars or 35,000 euros a year, your income is in the top 10% globally. And that group produces about half of household carbon pollution and also has enormous political, economic, cultural power.

Nick Petrić Howe: I was among those surprised to find myself in that group. Being in the 10% of income doesn’t quite gel with my, admittedly comfortable, but fairly ordinary life. It’s worth saying as well, that power and carbon emissions track income as it rises too. With around a fifth of warming between 1990 and 2020 attributable to people in the top 1% of income, and a bit under a tenth to those in the top 0.1%.

But the top 10%, which I’m going to guess includes a lot of you listening, still have a lot that they can do, according to Kimberly. She notes that things like reducing air travel, investing in low-emission funds, and switching to renewable energy providers could be effective. She’s even created a guide for people online where you can find what the highest impact climate actions you personally can take. She calls it finding your superpower.

Now, there are researchers who are critical of these ideas. Arguing that individual actions, like these, are a distraction from larger more systemic changes that should be taking place. And others have argued that the fossil fuel industry has used individual actions to take onus off themselves. In fact, carbon footprints — which focus on the emissions of an individual — were popularised by the fossil fuel industry.

But I spoke to a lot of different experts for this series, and they mostly agreed on both being important. We’ll need individual actions and systemic changes. And one doesn’t preclude the other. Things like individual actions may also actually lead to bigger changes.

This is also why Kimberly focuses on specific actions that she feels will have the biggest impacts. And one key one for those who live in a liberal democracy, where you can freely vote for your leaders, is to try and use your individual power to lead to systemic change.

Kimberly Nicholas: For those of us who do live in those countries, we have incredible powers like voting and encouraging and getting others to vote, mobilizing voting, joining a political party or organization that's taking powerful climate action. And the reason those types of actions are so important is that climate policies that affect everyone in a society, of course, have enormous potential, far bigger than, you know, our everyday lives at home, to really move the needle and dramatically decrease climate pollution.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it’s not just politics. This could also be things like engaging with climate action at work. Many workplaces have climate goals and there are usually other keen people you can connect with to try and make these goals happen. Maybe your own climate efforts are small, but a company of 10, 100 or thousands of people could make a much more tangible difference.

For example, there has been an employee-led effort to urge their companies to leave the US Chamber of Commerce. This business association rejected the scientific consensus on climate change until 2019 and has historically obstructed climate action. More recently, it has acknowledged that humans contribute to climate change, however, it still lobbied against the Inflation Reduction Act. So, climate concerned employees of the companies that are members of the Chamber have been petitioning their firms to leave the organisation. Many of those companies have now objected to the Chamber’s climate policies.

In fact, when I spoke to Kimberly it seemed that a lot of the ‘individual’ actions she suggested were really about connecting to others, be that political organising or simply socialising with other climate-conscious people. Those actions could build to something more, but they could also help with the reason I started this podcast in the first place. Anxiety.

Kimberly Nicholas: We want to make climate action fun. It should be something we look forward to and enjoy doing. That's one of the best parts of our week. and we know that from research, doing things together in community helps prevent burnout, it can help reduce anxiety, it can help motivate us and keep us going. And we all have ups and downs. I mean, we've all had moments of despair working on the climate crisis is not an easy thing to do. but we've also had moments of incredible elation and connection and creativity and joy. So being able to be in community is really powerful.

Nick Petrić Howe: And it could be that by connecting people together, that could ultimately lead to societal change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: I think there's this positive feedback loop by which all of our individual level actions can lead to bigger collective actions. And then collective actions can then trigger system level changes. The system level changes can then make it easier for individuals to take additional individual level actions because they would ideally remove the barriers to action.

Nick Petrić Howe: I have to admit that after my chat with Kimberley, I certainly felt a bit more empowered, but I was still a bit sceptical about the power of individuals. It’s not that I think individuals can’t do anything, it’s just the scale of the challenge that makes me hesitate. Even if I am, or even everyone listening is, the most climate conscious warriors in the world, it probably wouldn’t be enough. Like Kimberley alluded to, those individuals actions need to build towards the systemic. We need to change society.

I was curious about what the research said about the connection between the individual and the systemic and importantly, how can we actually get these small actions to help battle the global problem of climate change. So, I called up Madalina Vlasceanu, a social scientist who’s thought a lot about this exact issue.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So in my work we think about what are some ways in which collective action can be triggered at the individual level and then spread and catalyzed around groups and then collectives and then eventually making some system level pro changes.

Nick Petrić Howe: In our chat, one of the things that Madalina impressed upon me is that, while she believes that individual actions can lead to collective ones and then to systemic change, there are barriers that we need to acknowledge. For example, if you think the transition to renewable energy, the big barrier there is that fossil fuels are hugely subsidised. According to the International Monetary Fund, in 2024 fossil fuel subsidies were around $725 billion worldwide. If the underpricing of environmental costs are taken into account, such as air pollution and their contribution to climate change, that number rises to $6.7 trillion. In either case, fossil fuels are being made cheaper than they should be, which is not ideal when we should be using less of them.

Madalina Vlasceanu: So, our energy system needs to change and this can only happen through laws, policies, regulations that reduce, for example, fossil fuel subsidies currently valued at trillions of dollars. And in order for this to happen, for these systemic regulations to be introduced and enforced, there needs to, of course, be massive awareness campaigns from the public. So the public can push in this direction and make this direction the normative direction. So there is a big component here of the transition that has to do with laws, but the laws will likely change as an effect of pressure from the public.

Nick Petrić Howe: In fact, one reason that these subsidies persist is due to perceived unpopularity of raising the prices of fossil fuels — even if a switch to renewables would be cheaper in the long term. You may well have seen how people react to increases in heating or petrol costs. So, for politicians to make such changes, they’d need to believe that the public is on their side. Which is actually a strange position to be in, as most people do think that climate change is a big problem.

Research and polls show that the majority of people worldwide support climate action. So why do policymakers need convincing? Well, the problem is that support on a poll doesn’t necessarily translate to action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: There is a big difference between being aware of the problem in principle and being aware of this problem viscerally at a level where you know it's affecting you personally. So we know people have an optimism bias. and even though intellectually they can conceptualize that, well, there is this problem, people are talking about it, scientists are in agreement, it is going to get worse. And we understand that. At the same time, two things can be true. And so what is also true is that people think, well, this is probably not gonna affect me, or at least not very soon. And this is the type of thing where it'll probably happen first somewhere really far away or to other people or sometime in the pretty distant future. So I'd rather spend today or the near future thinking about more immediate issues that I have to worry about.

Nick Petrić Howe: I can certainly relate to spending my time worrying about things other than climate change. So, how do you actually get people to act? Madalina’s research has revealed some clues. By testing different interventions on a sample of 30,000 US citizens, she and a team of researchers were able to see what could actually get people to collectively act on climate change.

Madalina Vlasceanu: The top intervention leveraged two processes. So the two processes are efficacy beliefs and positive emotions. So efficacy beliefs means the belief that engaging in this activity will actually pay off in the exact way in which you're hoping it will. So the belief that if I do attend this protest, this protest will then reduce the risk of climate change. And so the way in which you can achieve this efficacy belief induction is by giving people examples of times in which such participation in collective action has actually had meaningful effects.

Nick Petrić Howe: Such examples include the banning of fossil fuel extraction in Quebec due to decades of grassroots movements and Los Angeles moving to ban urban oil extraction, because of years of protests and community organising.

Madalina Vlasceanu: And the other process I mentioned is positive emotions. So in addition to feeling like you will make a difference, you also need to feel like there is an emotional benefit to you personally, not just to the cause of the participation. So meaning-making, increasing belonging, or starting some close relationships with like-minded others. All of these more personal motivations to engage in collective action are also critical to engagement.

Nick Petrić Howe: Madalina also found that appealing to ideas like preserving the purity of the environment and respect for authority can also encourage more action — and these interventions were effective across the political spectrum.

To encourage more action, these interventions could be employed by governments, NGOs, charities and people making podcasts... They could say that you can make a difference, and you may even make some friends along the way. And by encouraging people to get together and act on climate, Madalina thinks we can create a positive feedback loop where more climate action is done, which makes it easier for us all to do more climate action.

Madalina Vlasceanu: It could be, for example, that someone's very motivated to not pollute very much or not use a lot of fossil fuels, but the system doesn't necessarily facilitate these actions. So it makes it much harder for me as an individual not to pollute, even if I wanted to. And so if I participate in collective action to change some of those systemic level decisions then it could be even easier for me to engage in individual level climate action by having an easier time engaging in in individual level behavioural change, such as you know, engaging in ways of transport that are less polluting.

If you’re sceptical about the power of groups of people, then we can take lessons from historical changes of the past. During the civil rights movement in the US, collections of small groups came together and organised protests, civil disobedience and boycotts that eventually led to new civil rights laws and the end of most legal discrimation against African Americans.

Madalina Vlasceanu: the main thing an individual can do to address climate change is to be less of an individual. And so we have to recognize the power in groups in the power of our collective to making change.

Nick Petrić Howe: So, if you want to fight climate change. Remember this. You can make a change, people have done it before, and it may even be good for you to do so.

Madalina Vlasceanu: Hopelessness is pretty natural, I would say. I felt hopelessness quite a lot at the beginning of this journey when I was first becoming aware of just how big the threat is. especially when I became a mother and I understood that my kids will inherit a very different world and a much worse one. Than I had. And so hopelessness is there. the one way I found to cope or to get out of it is by taking action. So action is the antidote to hopelessness.

Nick Petrić Howe: In this podcast series, I wanted to find out if there was anything I could do about climate change. And it turns out that perhaps things are not as bad as I thought. There are certainly challenges, and some big unknowns as to what might happen in the future.

But as humans, we have a tendency to focus on the negative. And when it comes to climate change, there’s plenty of negative to think about. Even if things are not as bad as I thought, we’re not really on track to meet our climate targets. We need more action, but perhaps that’s something in which we all have a role to play.

And according to the science, we can make a difference. I’m certainly trying to. [Since starting this podcast, I’ve changed my pension to be invested in climate-conscious way, joined a group organising for climate action in my company, and started talking more to people about climate. I’m talking to you right now. And that’s helped, with my anxiety. I just hope that it helps with the world.]

In the end, I turned my climate anxiety, into what I hope is a climate superpower — I’m still anxious but I’m using that energy to push me, to try and make difference. As Madalina said, Action is the antidote to hopelessness. I hope I’ve helped you feel a bit less hopeless.

For now, I’ll leave you with a final quote from Madalina.

Nick Petrić Howe: And then my last question is: how do we save the world?

Madalina Vlasceanu: Haha, good question. In my mind how we save the world is caring about each other and helping each other out.

Nick Petrić Howe: This podcast series was written and produced by me, Nick Petrić Howe. Dan Fox was my editor. Thanks also to Emma Lawrance, Kimberly Nicholas, Madalina Vlasceanu, and, of course, my mum for talking to me for this episode. And thank you all for listening too. If you like this sort of thing, then Kimberly has got her own climate podcast, I’ll link to that in the show notes as well.

#1052. NWSL announces new player development rule to incentivize youth investment, aims for further expansion

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The biggest week on the NWSL calendar is here as the buildup towards the 2026 NWSL Championship is underway. An awards show, countless events, and media days were all on the agenda ahead of Saturday's big game. That included the annual state of the league by commissioner Jessica Berman on Thursday.

This year, the commissioner welcomed media to the NWSL Championship in Washington, D.C., and celebrated record ticket sales, attendance, and future expansion ahead of Saturday night's championship between the Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current, live on CBS at 8 p.m. ET. She also announced a few new league rules and future match events.

The commissioner introduced the new player development rule. While the league previously submitted paperwork for a potential future second=division league, conversation and planning around that is currently paused with the upcoming 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and efforts to grow NWSL in other ways.

"As we grow from 16 to 18 teams in 2028, we know that we have to prioritize the pipeline, not just the pipeline of players, but the pipeline of talent that supports the players in the daily training environment. One of the things that makes the United States so uniquely positioned in the global women's soccer landscape is the depth of that potential pipeline," said Berman in her opening remarks.

"That's why today we're announcing the NWSL Player Development Rule. It's an important step in strengthening the pathway to professional soccer for the next generation of players. The rule creates actual incentives for clubs to invest in identifying, developing, and retaining young talent, and it gives the clubs the flexibility to design their programs in the way that makes sense with their sporting philosophies."

More information and the types of incentives will roll out for clubs as the new player development rule goes into effect, but it is another step in future roster-building for clubs now alongside general player signings, transfers, the High Impact Player rule, and the Under-18 mechanism.

The addition of the rule is paving the way for more support staff and systems in place. The commissioner also announced the new NWSL Sporting Executive Program, meant to provide more support for club leadership development. The inaugural set of leadership includes six executives from the league who will participate in the program.

"Developing the future of the sport is not just limited to the players; it's also about the technical staff who surround those players each and every day ... this is a first-of-its-kind program invested in talent, and it was curated and developed in collaboration with U.S. Soccer and FIFA. This new year-long initiative will provide sporting executives at our clubs with curated, specialized education, mentorship, and leadership development opportunities tailored around the unique demands of our league and the women's professional game," she said.

The NWSL commissioner then announced the future site of the next NWSL Challenge Cup. The 2027 NWSL Challenge Cup will take place in Austin, Texas, next summer.

The tournament has evolved since its first iteration as a placeholder for the COVID-19-affected season and is now a unique one-off marquee match between top clubs, typically the NWSL Shield titleholders and the NWSL Championship winners. In years where one club wins both, the game is a rematch of the previous NWSL Championship match.

"Following the success of this year's Challenge Cup in Columbus, where we took the event to a neutral site to give an opportunity to introduce the NWSL to a new community," she said.

The 2026 NWSL Challenge Cup was between 2025 NWSL Shield winners Kansas City Current and 2025 NWSL Championship winners Gotham FC. The 2026 competition was held in Columbus, Ohio. The state will now welcome its first NWSL franchise in 2028 alongside another expansion club in Atlanta.

Fans will undoubtedly make the connection and wonder if there is a future where an NWSL club calls Austin home. Currently, there are three NWSL clubs in California and only one in Texas, the Houston Dash.

"We're really excited to create another special experience for our fans and our players while making the NWSL a place that can invite new audiences," Berman said about heading to Austin.

Commissioner Berman celebrated the league's recent return to the nation's capital for another NWSL Championship. The city hosted the 2022 event and now returns four years later with more attention on the league, the clubs, and its players than ever before.

"Today, we're bigger, stronger, more visible, and more ambitious than ever before, and the next five years are going to redefine what's possible. We have an extraordinary opportunity in front of us, and we intend to seize it," she said.

Two incoming clubs set for 2028 and new player roster rules are just the beginning of NWSL's next chapter. There's still the potential for more clubs on the horizon, and current clubs Houston Dash and Racing Louisville are in the process of vetting for a sale to new ownership as franchise entry fees into the league are booming to new heights.

And of course, there is still the biggest game of the year to play on Saturday.

"The Washington Spirit are back in the championship for the third consecutive year, determined to bring home that title. And standing in their way is the Kansas City Current, with its own ambitions to win a championship after winning the Shield in 2025. These are two exceptional clubs, two incredibly passionate fan base, and the championship is still to be decided, [we're] very excited about the rest of this week."

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”
